questions.prompt: Two blocks sit one after the other. The first multiplies by 6 and the second multiplies by 5. The single block that replaces both multiplies by
questions.explanation: Blocks in series share one signal, so their gains multiply: \(6 \times 5 = 30\). Adding them gives 11, which is the parallel rule. Dividing them gives 1.2. Keeping only 6 drops the second block.

questions.prompt: Two blocks sit in parallel. One multiplies by 4 and the other by 7, and their outputs add. The equivalent gain is
questions.explanation: Parallel blocks see the same input and their outputs add, so the gain is \(4 + 7 = 11\). Multiplying would give 28, which is the series rule. Subtracting gives \(-3\) or \(3\), and neither block is subtracted here.

questions.prompt: A forward block \(G\) and a return block \(H\) form a negative feedback loop: the return signal is subtracted from the reference. The closed-loop gain from reference to output is
questions.explanation: Call the error \(e = r - Hy\) and the output \(y = Ge\). Substituting gives \(y = G(r - Hy)\), so \(y(1 + GH) = Gr\) and the gain is \(G/(1+GH)\). \(G+H\) adds the two blocks as if they were in parallel. The minus sign in the denominator is the positive-feedback formula. \(GH\) is the loop gain, not the closed-loop gain.

questions.prompt: Negative feedback. The forward gain is 8 and the return gain is 0.5. The closed-loop gain is
questions.explanation: The loop product is \(8 \times 0.5 = 4\). Negative feedback puts that product in the denominator: \(8/(1+4) = 1.6\). Using \(1 - 4\) changes the sign of the loop and is the positive-feedback formula. The product 4 itself is the loop gain, and \(8 + 0.5\) adds the blocks.

questions.prompt: Three signals are not involved: just two blocks in series, with gains 2.5 and 4. The equivalent gain is
questions.explanation: Series gains multiply: \(2.5 \times 4 = 10\). Adding gives 6.5. Dividing gives 0.625. The order does not matter for the product, but dropping either factor leaves 2.5 or 4.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 336 120" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>two series gains</title><line x1="24" y1="56" x2="60" y2="56"/><polygon points="60,56 53.6,58.7 53.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="60" y="34" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="102" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2.5</text><line x1="144" y1="56" x2="180" y2="56"/><polygon points="180,56 173.6,58.7 173.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="180" y="34" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="222" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">4</text><line x1="264" y1="56" x2="300" y2="56"/><polygon points="300,56 293.6,58.7 293.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="304" y="60" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">y</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: Two labeled blocks in a row, with arrows in and out.

questions.prompt: In a negative feedback loop the forward block is \(G\) and the return block is \(H\). Which expression is the loop gain?
questions.explanation: Start at the error and walk once around the loop: multiply by \(G\), then by \(H\), and you are back at the summing junction. That product \(GH\) is the loop gain. \(G\) skips the return path. \(G/(1+GH)\) is what the closed loop does to a reference. \(H\) is only the sensor path.

questions.figure_alt: A forward block and a return path that comes back to the input.

questions.prompt: The same blocks as a negative loop, but the return signal is added to the reference. Forward gain 2, return gain 0.2. The closed-loop gain is
questions.explanation: Positive feedback adds the return, so \(y = 2(r + 0.2 y)\). Then \(y(1 - 0.4) = 2r\) and the gain is \(2/0.6 = 3.333\). The negative-feedback formula \(2/(1+0.4) = 1.429\) subtracts a signal that this loop adds. The product 0.4 is the loop gain, and \(2 + 0.2\) adds the blocks as if they were side by side.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 234 140" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>positive feedback</title><text x="24" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">r</text><line x1="42" y1="56" x2="78" y2="56"/><polygon points="78,56 71.6,58.7 71.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="78" y="34" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="120" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2</text><line x1="162" y1="56" x2="198" y2="56"/><polygon points="198,56 191.6,58.7 191.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="202" y="60" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">y</text><line x1="190" y1="56" x2="190" y2="100"/><line x1="190" y1="100" x2="40" y2="100"/><line x1="40" y1="100" x2="40" y2="72"/><polygon points="40,72 42.7,78.4 37.3,78.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="119" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0.2</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A forward block and a return path that comes back to the input.

questions.prompt: A disturbance adds at the output, after the forward block. The loop gain is \(L\). The fraction of that disturbance still present at the output is
questions.explanation: With the reference held at zero, \(y = d - L y\), because the loop sees the output and drives back against it. Then \(y(1+L) = d\), so the fraction is \(1/(1+L)\). \(L\) and \(1+L\) grow as the loop gets stronger, but a stronger loop rejects more of \(d\). \(L/(1+L)\) is the fraction of a reference that gets through, not of a disturbance.

questions.prompt: Three blocks in series have gains 2, 3, and 4. The equivalent gain is
questions.explanation: Each block multiplies the signal that leaves the previous one, so the gains multiply: \(2 \times 3 \times 4 = 24\). Adding gives 9. Multiplying only the first pair leaves 6, and only the last pair leaves 12.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 456 120" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>three series blocks</title><line x1="24" y1="56" x2="60" y2="56"/><polygon points="60,56 53.6,58.7 53.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="60" y="34" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="102" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2</text><line x1="144" y1="56" x2="180" y2="56"/><polygon points="180,56 173.6,58.7 173.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="180" y="34" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="222" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">3</text><line x1="264" y1="56" x2="300" y2="56"/><polygon points="300,56 293.6,58.7 293.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="300" y="34" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="342" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">4</text><line x1="384" y1="56" x2="420" y2="56"/><polygon points="420,56 413.6,58.7 413.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="424" y="60" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">y</text></svg>

questions.prompt: A loop you will later write as one transfer function has forward gain 9 and return gain 2, with the return subtracted. The closed-loop gain is
questions.explanation: The loop gain is \(9 \times 2 = 18\). Negative feedback gives \(9/(1+18) = 9/19 = 0.4737\). The product 18 is the loop gain, not the closed-loop gain. \(9/(1-18)\) flips the feedback sign. \(9+2\) adds the two paths.

questions.figure_alt: A forward block and a return path that comes back to the input.

questions.prompt: The loop gain is 4. A disturbance adds at the output. The fraction of it that remains is
questions.explanation: Hold the reference at zero. Then \(y = d - 4y\), so \(y = d/5 = 0.2\). The complementary fraction \(4/5 = 0.8\) is how much of a reference would get through, not how much of \(d\) remains. Leaving the 4 un-normalized reports the loop gain itself.

questions.figure_alt: A forward block and a return path that comes back to the input.

questions.prompt: The product you would plot as a loop gain is made of three series blocks, 1.5, 2, and 4. That product is
questions.explanation: The loop gain is the product of every block you meet on one trip around the loop. Here that trip is three blocks: \(1.5 \times 2 \times 4 = 12\). Adding gives 7.5. The first pair alone is 3, and the last pair alone is 8.
